stories.headline: Update: Meta Agrees to Pay Up to $18 Billion to Settle Child Safety Claims Brought by 29 States
stories.summary:
Meta has agreed to pay up to $18 billion to settle a lawsuit brought by 29 U.S. states alleging that its Facebook and Instagram platforms caused harm to children through addictive design features and privacy violations. The settlement, which stems from a 2023 lawsuit, would be among the largest consumer protection settlements in U.S. history. A federal judge indicated she is likely to approve the deal, though it has not yet received final court approval.

Under the terms, Meta must introduce new safeguards for teenage users, including daily usage limits and nighttime blocks set on by default. Meta has contested the underlying claims throughout the litigation, maintaining it is committed to child safety on its platforms. The company has stipulated that 30% of the $18 billion will only be released if competitors YouTube and TikTok implement comparable measures.

The settlement resolves a legal battle that accelerated a national debate over social media's effects on youth mental health. Advocates for children's safety called the agreement a landmark moment, though some psychologists cautioned its practical impact may be limited if similar rules are not applied uniformly across competing platforms. State attorneys general framed the deal as a signal to the entire industry.

Note: An earlier digest entry referenced a $17 billion figure from a prior stage of the settlement; today's filing and court proceedings confirmed the figure of up to $18 billion, representing a material update to the previously covered story.

stories.headline: Ratko Mladic, 'Butcher of Bosnia' Convicted of Genocide, Dies at 84 in UN Custody
stories.summary:
Ratko Mladic, the Bosnian Serb military commander convicted of genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity for his role in the 1990s Balkan wars, died Thursday at age 84 while serving a life sentence at a UN detention facility in The Hague, Netherlands. The UN tribunal confirmed his death. Mladic had been in declining health for years.

Mladic commanded the Army of Republika Srpska during the Bosnian War and oversaw the siege of Sarajevo — the longest siege of a capital city in modern warfare — as well as the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, in which approximately 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys were systematically killed, the worst mass atrocity in Europe since World War II. He was arrested in Serbia in 2011 after more than 15 years as a fugitive and convicted in 2017.

His death closes a chapter on one of the most consequential war crimes prosecutions of the post-Cold War era. Survivors and victims' groups in Bosnia, particularly from Srebrenica, reacted to the news with mixed emotions — many expressing relief that he died in custody, while others lamented that he never expressed remorse. The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia had long been seen as a test case for international accountability for mass atrocities.

stories.headline: Gaza Ceasefire Under Severe Strain as Trump Peace Board Envoy Warns of 'Point of No Return'
stories.summary:
A senior official on President Trump's Board of Peace delivered a stark warning to the UN Security Council on Wednesday, saying the collapse of the Gaza ceasefire — brokered by the U.S. last October — would represent "a point of no return" for the region. Nickolay Mladenov, the Board's high representative for Gaza, criticized both Israel's continued airstrikes, which have killed more than 1,300 Palestinians including 300 children since the ceasefire began, and Hamas's failure to fully cease military activities.

At the heart of the impasse is a fundamental disagreement over sequencing: Hamas has agreed to disarm in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal, but Israel insists full Hamas disarmament must precede any pullout. Mladenov described the process as "sequenced and reciprocal," but Trump envoy Jared Kushner recently appeared to shift the U.S. position closer to Israel's, saying withdrawal would only be discussed once demilitarization was "done."

Israel rejected the Board of Peace's 15-point Hamas disarmament roadmap last month. The Israeli military says four of its soldiers have been killed in Palestinian attacks during the same period covered by the ceasefire. The divergence between Kushner's and Mladenov's public statements has raised questions about internal coherence within the Trump administration's approach to the Gaza file.

stories.headline: Update: USPS Mail-In Voting Rules Take Effect; 24 States Sue as Midterm Legal Battle Intensifies
stories.summary:
The U.S. Postal Service confirmed Thursday that new requirements for mail-in voting ballots are now in effect, a move that came days after the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration's restrictions to stand ahead of November's midterm elections. The rules represent a significant tightening of mail ballot procedures and are expected to generate a fresh wave of legal challenges.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro joined 23 other states in filing a lawsuit against the USPS, arguing that Congress — not the president or the Postal Service — has constitutional authority to set federal election rules. The lawsuit is the latest front in a broader conflict between the Trump administration and Democratic-led states over voting procedures, with the administration separately pushing states to submit voter rolls for federal inspection as a condition of receiving police and anti-terrorism funding.

Supporters of the new rules argue they are necessary to maintain election integrity and reduce fraud, while critics — including voting rights groups and state election officials — contend the measures are designed to suppress turnout and sow confusion ahead of a consequential midterm. With control of both the House and Senate potentially at stake, the legal and political battle over mail-in voting is now one of the defining conflicts of the 2026 election cycle.

stories.headline: Update: Strait of Hormuz Deal Inches Closer as Oil Prices Dip; U.S. Commits to Tehran Sanctions
stories.summary:
Diplomatic momentum toward a resolution of the U.S.-Iran standoff over the Strait of Hormuz accelerated Thursday, with oil prices declining on reports that a framework agreement may be within reach. The United States simultaneously committed to a new package of sanctions against Tehran, a dual-track approach of pressure and negotiation that has defined the administration's strategy throughout the crisis.

The situation continues to affect energy markets globally, with gas prices remaining above $4 per gallon in the United States — a persistent drag on consumer confidence. Azerbaijan, whose Nakhchivan exclave was struck by Iranian drones in March, has emerged as a secondary flashpoint, with analysts noting that Baku's close military ties with Israel have drawn Iranian suspicion despite Azerbaijan's formal neutrality.

Supporters of the administration's approach argue the sanctions commitment demonstrates that Washington is not offering concessions under duress, while critics contend that maintaining economic pressure while negotiating risks collapsing any emerging deal. The standoff has now lasted weeks, disrupting global shipping and drawing in regional actors across the Middle East and South Caucasus.

The story is being tracked by 32 outlets, making it one of the most widely covered international developments of the day. No formal ceasefire or agreement has been announced, and officials on both sides have cautioned that talks remain fragile.

stories.headline: Update: Federal Judge Clears Path for ICE Agent Christian Castro's Release, Rejects Minnesota's Emergency Request
stories.summary:
A federal judge in Texas on Wednesday rejected Minnesota's emergency bid to block the release of ICE agent Christian Castro, whose 90-day detention period under Texas law expires Thursday. U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. ruled that Minnesota failed to satisfy the legal requirements for a temporary restraining order, finding the case was not yet ripe because Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has neither agreed to nor denied the state's extradition request.

Castro was arrested in Cameron County on a Minnesota warrant stemming from a shooting of a Venezuelan immigrant during an immigration enforcement operation in Minneapolis. Minnesota had argued urgently that without a court order, Castro could flee to Mexico, citing jail calls in which he discussed buying property there. The judge acknowledged Abbott had taken an "atypically-long duration" to review the matter but found no legal deadline requiring him to act faster.

The case has become a flashpoint in the broader national debate over immigration enforcement and state-versus-federal authority. Abbott and Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison have traded sharp public criticism — Abbott's office calling the prosecution a "political stunt," while Ellison and Minnesota officials argue that no law enforcement officer is above the law. The Department of Homeland Security has also weighed in, defending Castro's conduct.

The ruling means Castro is expected to walk free Thursday barring a last-minute reversal. Minnesota retains the option of pursuing extradition through other channels, but the path forward is now significantly more complicated, with Castro potentially out of custody and the extradition question unresolved.

stories.headline: State Department Designates Italy-Based Tech Collective Autistici/Inventati as Global Terrorist Organization Over Antifa, Hamas Ties
stories.summary:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced Wednesday that the United States has designated Autistici/Inventati — an Italy-based technology collective — as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist entity. The State Department's action freezes any U.S.-jurisdiction assets the group holds and bars Americans and U.S. financial institutions from transacting with it, with violators subject to civil or criminal penalties.

According to a State Department memo obtained by Fox News Digital, the collective provided encrypted communications, web hosting, secure video conferencing, and anonymity tools to violent far-left organizations in the United States and Europe, as well as to Islamic terrorist groups including Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The memo specifically names Portland-based Rose City Antifa as a domestic group that relied on the collective's infrastructure, and links a media organization using the collective's tools to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine.

The designation represents an escalation of the Trump administration's stated policy of treating far-left extremism as a formal terrorism threat, following a September 2025 executive order designating Antifa a domestic terrorist organization. Rubio said "far-left terrorism poses a profound threat to the United States and the broader West." Civil liberties advocates and critics of the administration are likely to challenge the designation, raising concerns about the government applying terrorism labels to political infrastructure and free-speech-adjacent services.

The action is exclusively reported by Fox News Digital based on a leaked internal State Department memo. Independent corroboration of the specific claims in the memo was not immediately available from other outlets.

stories.headline: Thieves Steal Bronze Age Gold Artifacts from Spanish Museum in Four-Minute Heist
stories.summary:
Thieves executed a brazen predawn raid on the Villena Museum in Spain's Alicante province early Friday, stealing the majority of the Treasure of Villena — a collection of nearly 10 kilograms of Bronze Age gold artifacts dating to approximately 1,000 BC. The haul included rings, bowls, and bracelets from a trove of more than 60 objects, considered one of the most significant prehistoric gold collections in the world.

The operation was carried out in roughly four minutes, after thieves first triggered a false alarm at a nearby sports center to divert police. By the time officers responded to the museum's alarm at around 5:20 a.m. local time, the thieves had already fled. Villena Mayor Fulgencio Cerdán confirmed that "most of the treasure" — specifically all the gold items — had been taken, calling it devastating for the community. A town council spokesman insisted all security systems had been properly activated.

The heist is the latest in a wave of high-profile museum thefts across Europe. In October 2025, thieves stole jewelry worth $102 million from the Louvre in Paris in broad daylight. Last week, four works by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina were stolen from a Sicilian museum, and Italian police recently recovered paintings by Renoir, Cézanne, and Matisse stolen from a foundation near Parma.

Spanish police are assessing exactly how many items were taken and have not yet announced arrests or suspects. The Treasure of Villena was discovered in 1963 by archaeologist José María Soler in a dried riverbed and has been housed at the Villena Museum since. Its loss would represent one of the most significant thefts of prehistoric European artifacts in modern history.

stories.headline: Update: CIA Director Ratcliffe's Moscow Trip Was Warning to Russia Not to Attack NATO
stories.summary:
New details have emerged about CIA Director John Ratcliffe's unannounced visit to Moscow this week: sources familiar with the trip told ABC News and others that a central purpose was to warn Russia not to attack NATO member states, amid U.S. intelligence assessments that Moscow could attempt to test the alliance's resolve. The disclosure adds significant context to a visit that had sparked widespread speculation since it was first reported.

President Trump downplayed the trip as 'semi-routine,' while Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna sought to minimize its significance, saying the threat Russia poses to Baltic nations had not changed. The visit was nonetheless extraordinary by historical standards, with a U.S. intelligence chief traveling directly to Moscow on a government transport aircraft.

The warning comes as Russia's war in Ukraine continues and as NATO allies face ongoing questions about American commitment to collective defense. The revelation that Ratcliffe delivered a direct deterrence message — rather than, as some had speculated, seeking Russian support for Iran pressure — may reassure European partners who have grown anxious about U.S. foreign policy direction under the Trump administration.

The Ratcliffe visit is the latest in a series of high-stakes diplomatic moves involving the administration, which has simultaneously been managing a standoff with Iran, trade conflict with Canada, and persistent tensions along NATO's eastern flank.

stories.headline: 9/11 Accused Plotters Set for Trial in June 2028, More Than 26 Years After Attacks
stories.summary:
A military judge set a tentative June 2028 trial date for Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and three co-defendants accused of planning the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, which killed nearly 3,000 people. Air Force Lt. Col. Michael Schrama issued the order on Wednesday, meaning the trial — if it proceeds on schedule — would begin nearly 27 years after the attacks and 20 years after the defendants were first arraigned in 2008.

The path to trial has been repeatedly disrupted. Plea deals that would have spared Mohammed and two co-defendants the death penalty were negotiated but subsequently voided after the Trump administration intervened. Legal battles over evidence, the admissibility of statements obtained under interrogation, and the structure of the military commissions system have contributed to decades of delays.

The case remains one of the most consequential and legally complex in American history, pitting national security considerations — including classified evidence and the legacy of post-9/11 detention and interrogation programs — against defendants' constitutional and legal rights. Critics across the political spectrum have long argued the prolonged pre-trial period represents a failure of the military justice system.

Families of victims have waited more than two decades for a verdict. Whether the 2028 date holds will depend on further pretrial litigation, the health of elderly defendants, and potential additional legal challenges from both prosecution and defense.

stories.headline: Surrogacy Custody Battle in Texas Draws National Attention Over Abortion, Parental Rights
stories.summary:
A Texas court this week heard arguments in a high-profile custody dispute between a California couple and their surrogate, who refused to terminate a pregnancy after the fetus was diagnosed with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a serious congenital heart defect. The case involves Nausheen Gilkar and Omar Ahmed, biological parents who say they requested an abortion after the diagnosis, and surrogate McKenna West, an Alaska nurse who declined and subsequently gave birth.

West testified she was connected with an anti-abortion group after the dispute arose; the group arranged legal representation, flew her to Texas — where abortion is banned — and is covering her legal costs. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton also intervened. A California court ruled in June that Gilkar and Ahmed are the legal parents, but West is seeking to overturn that ruling and gain custody of the child, who has already undergone surgery.

The case has drawn competing advocacy from both sides of the abortion debate. Anti-abortion groups argue surrogacy contracts should not compel abortion decisions. Reproductive rights advocates argue the case illustrates how abortion restrictions in some states can override agreements made in other jurisdictions, creating interstate legal conflicts.

The dispute touches several unresolved areas of American law: the enforceability of surrogacy contracts across state lines, the extent to which biological parentage determines legal custody, and the intersection of surrogacy with abortion policy in a post-Dobbs legal landscape.

stories.headline: NFL Abolishes Pro Bowl Game After More Than 70 Years
stories.summary:
The NFL announced Wednesday that it is ending the Pro Bowl game, discontinuing the all-star exhibition that had been held in some form almost every year since 1951. The decision was made at the league's owners' meeting in Atlanta. The game was last held in its tackle format in 2022 before switching to flag football in 2023 in an attempt to reverse declining interest.

Despite the elimination of the game, 88 players per season will still be designated as Pro Bowlers and honored at a ceremony in Los Angeles. The league will also hold flag football events at that time. NFL executive vice president Peter O'Reilly framed the move as returning the Pro Bowl selection to its original purpose as an honor rather than a competitive event.

League officials cited feedback from players who said they did not want competitive play following the physical demands of a full season and playoffs. Troy Vincent, the NFL's executive vice president of football operations, said players felt an all-star game could not adequately replicate the intensity of championship-level play and risked injuries without meaningful stakes.

The Pro Bowl had been held for most of its history in Honolulu before the league rotated the event to various cities in recent years. Its cancellation ends one of the longest-running traditions in American professional sports.
